C005.subject: Smaller class sizes for K-3 students from low-income households
C005.object: standardized test scores more than for students from higher-income households
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Smaller class sizes for K-3 students from low-income households standardized test scores more than for students from higher-income households]

[PATH:empirical] Reanalysis of Project STAR data with interaction terms for free/reduced-price lunch status and class size — Project STAR is the key experimental dataset; reanalyzing it with explicit socioeconomic interaction terms can directly test whether low-income students benefit more in test scores from smaller classes than higher-income peers.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal studies of California's Class Size Reduction (CSR) program, comparing achievement gaps by income level over time — California's statewide CSR policy provides a natural experiment with large, diverse populations; tracking differential effects across income groups can confirm or refute the hypothesized differential benefit.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class-size effects on standardized test scores with moderator analysis for socioeconomic status — A systematic review and meta-analysis that pools estimates from multiple studies (e.g., Project STAR, Wisconsin SAGE, Florida CSR) and tests whether effect sizes significantly differ by income level would provide robust evidence for or against the hypothesis.

scope.domain: early elementary education (K-3), with socioeconomic stratification

qualifier.temporal: 1990–2020, primarily studies from Project STAR and similar U.S. experiments
qualifier.geographic: United States, especially states with class-size reduction policies (e.g., Tennessee, California, Florida)

C006.subject: Smaller class sizes for K-3 students
C006.object: standardized test scores in early elementary grades
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Smaller class sizes for K-3 students standardized test scores in early elementary grades]

[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal dataset — This randomized controlled trial from Tennessee (1985-1989) provides direct causal evidence on class size effects on K-3 standardized test scores. Re-analyzing the data with modern statistical methods can clarify the magnitude and persistence of effects, directly testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of class size reduction studies (e.g., Hattie's Visible Learning or the What Works Clearinghouse review) — A systematic synthesis of multiple studies post-2000 in the U.S. can reveal the overall effect size and heterogeneity. If the meta-analytic average is near zero, it would support the hypothesis; if positive, it would refute it.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies using state-level policy variation (e.g., California's Class Size Reduction program, 1996) — Analyzing test score trends before and after large-scale policy changes, while controlling for confounding factors (e.g., teacher quality, funding shifts), provides real-world evidence on whether smaller classes improve outcomes in diverse U.S. contexts since 2000.

C007.subject: Teacher quality and instructional practices
C007.object: the negative effect of large class sizes on standardized test scores when class size exceeds 30 students
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Teacher quality and instructional practices the negative effect of large class sizes on standardized test scores when class size exceeds 30 students]

[PATH:empirical] Reanalysis of STAR class-size experiment data with interaction terms for teacher effectiveness and class size thresholds above 30 — The Tennessee STAR experiment provides randomized variation in class size; reanalyzing with a spline or interaction model can test whether the negative effect of large classes disappears when teacher quality is high, specifically above the 30-student threshold.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on class size effects and teacher quality interactions (e.g., from the What Works Clearinghouse or Hattie's Visible Learning database) — A systematic review of existing meta-analyses can identify whether the hypothesized threshold effect (class size > 30) and full suppression by teacher quality is supported or contradicted by the aggregate evidence across multiple contexts.

[PATH:empirical] Causal inference using longitudinal administrative data with teacher value-added measures and class size shocks — Using within-school, within-teacher variation in class sizes (e.g., due to enrollment fluctuations) and high-quality teacher effectiveness estimates, one can test whether the class size penalty is nullified for highly effective teachers when classes exceed 30 students.

qualifier.tension: Refines the original claim by specifying a threshold above which teacher quality becomes the sole determinant, eliminating the class size effect entirely.

C008.subject: Class size reduction
C008.predicate: has a direct and significant impact on

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Class size reduction standardized test scores irrespective of teacher quality]

[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal study data re-analysis — This randomized controlled trial in Tennessee provides the strongest causal evidence on class size effects. Re-analyzing the data while controlling for teacher quality measures (e.g., value-added scores, credentials) can directly test whether class size reduction impacts test scores independently of teacher quality.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size studies with teacher quality covariates — A systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizing studies that simultaneously estimate class size and teacher quality effects on standardized test scores would clarify the extent to which class size effects persist after accounting for teacher quality, addressing the disputed claim.

C009.subject: Teacher quality and instructional practices
C009.object: the direct effect of class size on standardized test scores when class size exceeds 25 students
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Teacher quality and instructional practices the direct effect of class size on standardized test scores when class size exceeds 25 students]

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) experiment data, focusing on classrooms with >25 students and controlling for teacher quality metrics (e.g., value-added scores or observational ratings). — The STAR experiment is a classic randomized trial on class size effects. Re-analyzing its data with a threshold of 25 and including teacher quality measures can directly test whether the class-size effect disappears in larger classes when teacher quality is accounted for.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size and teacher effectiveness studies, stratified by class size categories (e.g., <20, 20-25, >25) and controlling for instructional quality. — A systematic review and meta-analysis can synthesize existing evidence across multiple studies to determine whether the hypothesized threshold effect is consistently observed, thereby confirming or refuting the claim that teacher quality completely supplants class size effects above 25 students.

[PATH:empirical] Causal inference modeling using administrative data from a large school district, applying instrumental variables or propensity score matching to isolate the interaction between class size (>25) and teacher quality on test scores. — Observational data with rich covariates (e.g., teacher experience, certification, prior student achievement) can be used to model the causal effect of class size conditional on teacher quality. This approach can identify whether the direct effect of class size becomes null when teacher quality is high in larger classes.

qualifier.tension: Refines the original claim by specifying a threshold above which teacher quality becomes the sole driver, eliminating any independent class size effect.

[PATH:empirical] Tennessee STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) experiment — This large-scale randomized controlled trial directly tests class size effects on test scores, providing causal evidence to compare against teacher quality and instructional practices.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size and student achievement (e.g., Hattie's Visible Learning or meta-analyses by Glass & Smith) — Synthesizes multiple studies to quantify effect sizes of class size relative to teacher quality and instructional practices, clarifying which factor has a more significant impact.

[PATH:empirical] Value-added modeling studies comparing teacher effectiveness and class size effects on standardized test scores — These studies use longitudinal data to isolate the relative contributions of class size versus teacher quality, directly addressing the disputed comparison.
